body.text: A necklace made of gold nuggets, tableware and a bronze cherub.
All three came from the wreckage of the Titanic, and for 40 years, selling them was illegal.
Now, a company that has controlled the salvage rights to the famous shipwreck for more than 30 years wants to auction off more than 100 artefacts. The US government is fighting to stop it.
First, catch me up
More than a century after the Titanic sank, questions about who controls the ship's recovered artefacts and what should become of them are back before the courts.
Only one company holds exclusive salvage rights to the iconic shipwreck in the North Atlantic: RMS Titanic Incorporated. A US court granted those rights in 1994.
The catch? The company agreed to preserve the collection as a whole, rather than sell off individual items, so that the artefacts would be studied and displayed for the public.
But that changed earlier this year.
In March, a Virginia court considered a proposal from RMS Titanic Inc to auction more than 100 artefacts from its collection.
Among the items are pieces of gem-studded jewellery, cutlery and a bronze cherub that once adorned the vessel's grand staircase.
Since then, RMS Titanic Inc and the US government have been locked in a legal battle over whether the sale should be allowed.
What's the argument?
One side wants the collection kept whole forever. The other sees 100 priceless objects, some of which could sell for millions.
Following RMS Titanic Inc's filing in March, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), which represents the US in the case, filed a response opposing the plan.
They believe selling the artefacts would violate RMS Titanic's legal obligations to the site.

"The public interest strongly favours maintaining all artefacts … together as an intact collection that is available to posterity for public purposes. It is also indisputable that, over several decades, RMST has repeatedly committed to do just that," according to a government filing.
Historians and archaeologists have also opposed the plan, warning that once this history is split up and sold, it is gone for good.
But RMS Titanic Inc argues the artefacts it wants to sell are different.
The company said the objects come from what is known as the "French Collection", a group of items recovered during a 1987 expedition carried out by a predecessor company and the French government.
According to a court filing, RMS Titanic Inc said those artefacts were not covered by the same court-imposed restrictions as items recovered in later salvage missions.

In a statement to The New York Times, lawyer Brian Wainger said the company believes that "the law of the case permit the sale of these artefacts and that such sale is consistent with its obligations as a respectful steward of the artefacts collections".
He declined to explain why the company wanted to sell the items.

In August, US District Judge Rebecca Beach Smith temporarily blocked the sale, saying she needed more information before deciding whether the proposal violated the conditions attached to the company's salvage rights.
But RMS Titanic appealed to the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals and asked for a fast-track consideration of its plan to sell the artefacts on October 9.
It plans to file an opening brief to that court.

It is not the first time RMS Titanic Inc has attempted to sell artefacts. A similar proposal in 2016, made while the company was facing bankruptcy proceedings, also drew objections from the US and French governments, UNESCO and cultural institutions.
Strong demand for Titanic memorabilia
The legal fight is unfolding against a backdrop of strong demand for Titanic artefacts.
Since 1987, when the shipwreck was first salvaged, thousands of items have been retrieved from the Titanic.
RMS Titanic Inc largely earns revenue by exhibiting those artefacts around the world.

Over the years, the company has argued that selling some items could help fund future operations. Courts and preservation groups have generally resisted those efforts, particularly because many recovered belongings once belonged to Titanic passengers.
However, artefacts that never formed part of the salvaged collection can be sold and often fetch big sums.

In April, a life jacket worn by a passenger as she escaped the sinking steamship sold at auction for more than $US900,000 ($1.28 million). A seat cushion from one of the Titanic lifeboats sold at the same Henry Aldridge & Son auction for $527,000.
In 2025, a gold pocket watch recovered from the body of wealthy passenger Isidor Straus sold for £1.78 million ($3.6 million), setting a record for Titanic memorabilia.
In 2013, a violin believed to have been played as the ship sank sold for $1.45 million.
Auctioneers say the Titanic's enduring appeal and the scarcity of genuine artefacts continue to attract buyers willing to pay premium prices.
What happened to the Titanic?
About 1,500 people died when the Titanic hit an iceberg on the night of 14 April 1912, during its maiden voyage from Southampton to New York.
The ship sank in the early hours of April 15 and now rests about 640 kilometres off the coast of Newfoundland, Canada, roughly four kilometres beneath the surface of the North Atlantic Ocean.
About 700 people survived the disaster, although the exact number was never confirmed.
